findings.highlight: The lights finally go out in the noisy tatami-floored room, and silence returns.
findings.evidenceJa: セイバーに何が起こっていたのか、さっきまでとんでもなく賑やかだった座敷の明かりが消えて、静寂が戻ってきた。
findings.governingReading: Whatever had been happening to Saber, the lights in the room that was extraordinarily lively until moments ago go out and silence returns.
findings.explanation: The English omits the opening reference to what Saber may have been subjected to in the women’s room and weakens the immediate contrast from “until just now” and “outrageously lively” to merely noisy.

findings.highlight: It’s not good for my mental health to have girls my age being rowdy in the same house.
findings.evidenceJa: すぐ近く、同じ屋根の下で同年輩の女の子たちが騒いでいた、というのは精神衛生上よろしくない。
findings.governingReading: For Shirou’s peace of mind, it is unhealthy to have girls his own age making noise very nearby under the same roof.
findings.explanation: “In the same house” drops すぐ近く, the immediate physical proximity that drives Shirou’s sexual and social self-consciousness.

findings.highlight: whether Fuji-nee is thinking at all or not.
findings.evidenceJa: そもそも藤ねえは何を考えているのか
findings.governingReading: Shirou wonders, fundamentally, what Taiga is thinking.
findings.explanation: The English changes the object of Taiga’s thought into a joke that she may not think at all, adding a sharper insult absent from the source.

findings.highlight: I quietly make my way to the door so I won’t wake them up.
findings.evidenceJa: 足音を殺して部屋の襖に手をかけた。
findings.governingReading: Silencing his footsteps so the sleeping women will not notice, Shirou puts his hand on his room’s sliding door.
findings.explanation: The English turns a completed, precise stealth action at the fusuma into merely moving toward a generic door and changes avoiding detection into avoiding waking them.

findings.evidenceJa: 切りつける風は冷たい。
findings.governingReading: The wind that cuts against him is cold.
findings.explanation: The English drops the cutting physical action of the wind and leaves only temperature, weakening the hostile winter-night atmosphere.

findings.evidenceJa: おんぼろなストーブに火を入れた。
findings.governingReading: Shirou lights the battered old stove.
findings.explanation: The English omits the stove’s decrepit condition and renders lighting it as the generic “turn on,” smoothing the shed’s material poverty.

findings.highlight: The teaching of archery focuses on accuracy, piercing strength, and endurance.
findings.evidenceJa: 弓道における中貫久の教え。
findings.governingReading: This is the kyudo teaching called chū-kan-kyū: hitting, penetration, and sustained continuance.
findings.explanation: The English converts a named three-part doctrine into a generic statement about what archery focuses on, erasing the term that structures Shirou’s analogy for continued magecraft training.

findings.highlight: I think there was something in an archery manual…
findings.evidenceJa: たしか中要秘刊集あたりにあった言葉だ。
findings.governingReading: Shirou recalls that the saying appeared in a work around the Chūyō Hikan-shū.
findings.explanation: The English replaces the specifically remembered title with an indefinite “an archery manual,” weakening Shirou’s textual knowledge and the quotation’s provenance.

findings.highlight: My mind imagines the same thing. An image of a sword that pops into my brain.
findings.evidenceJa: 脳裏にはいつもの映像。空っぽの頭に浮かび上がる剣の姿。
findings.governingReading: The familiar image is before his mind: the form of a sword rising into an emptied head.
findings.explanation: “My mind imagines” makes Shirou actively generate the image, while “pops into my brain” is casual and involuntary; together they obscure the disciplined emptying and emergence central to his ritual.

findings.highlight: I have to repeat it before I forget the sensation.
findings.evidenceJa: その感覚を忘れないうちに繰り返して、確実にモノにしなければ勿体ない。
findings.governingReading: He must repeat the spell before the sensation fades and make the technique securely his own; failing to capitalize on the success would be a waste.
findings.explanation: The English preserves repetition before forgetting but omits the goal of reliable mastery and the evaluative reason that letting the opportunity pass would be wasteful.

findings.highlight: I narrow my eyes and breathe out.
findings.evidenceJa: 目を半眼にして肺の中身を絞り出す。
findings.governingReading: Shirou lets his eyes fall half-lidded and squeezes the contents from his lungs.
findings.explanation: The English changes the meditative half-lidded gaze into narrowed eyes and reduces forceful, complete lung-emptying to ordinary exhalation, weakening the bodily ritual.

findings.highlight: I’ll forget about the Holy Grail War, Saber, and Tohsaka once I start this process.
findings.evidenceJa: この工程に没すれば全てなくなる。
findings.governingReading: Once Shirou immerses himself in this process, the Grail War, Saber, Tohsaka—everything—ceases to exist for him.
findings.explanation: “I’ll forget” turns the disappearance produced by total immersion into a deliberate memory action and weakens 没すれば, being absorbed or submerged in the process, to merely starting it.

findings.highlight: I clear my head from all hesitations.
findings.evidenceJa: 未熟な自分の迷いを一切忘れるほど思考を無にしなくてはならない。
findings.governingReading: He must reduce thought to nothing so completely that he forgets every hesitation of his immature self.
findings.explanation: The English omits Shirou’s self-judgment as immature, the degree/result construction, and the necessity of reaching thoughtlessness; it reports generic clearing as a simple action.

findings.highlight: The thought that Tohsaka might be doing the same training never escapes my head.
findings.evidenceJa: 自分がこうしている今、魔術師である遠坂も同じように鍛錬をしているのかとそんな雑念が、頭から離れなかった。
findings.governingReading: An intrusive thought will not leave him: right now, as he trains this way, might Tohsaka—the magus—be undergoing similar discipline?
findings.explanation: The English drops the simultaneity with Shirou’s present act, Tohsaka’s identity as a magus, and 雑念’s judgment that this is distracting mental noise intruding on the emptiness he seeks.

findings.highlight: Damn. My sleepiness went away thinking about them.
findings.evidenceJa: くそ。気になって眠気なんてなくなった
findings.governingReading: Damn. Being bothered by the situation made his sleepiness disappear.
findings.explanation: 気になって describes being unable to stop worrying about or being preoccupied by the matter, not simply thinking about it. The English makes “thinking about them” the mechanism and loses Shirou's anxious, involuntary preoccupation that drives the following list.

findings.highlight: Something about continuing forever after one masters the true meaning of archery.
findings.evidenceJa: 一度射手たらんと志す者は、真の意味を具備した後にこれを永久に続ける事なり。
findings.governingReading: A person who once resolves to become an archer must continue this practice forever after acquiring its true meaning.
findings.explanation: The English omits the subject's initial aspiration to become an archer and leaves “continuing forever” without a clear object. It also turns 具備した into mastering the “true meaning of archery,” while the source's formal maxim concerns the practitioner continuing the described discipline after attaining its meaning.

findings.highlight: …And how one should shoot more than 200 arrows a day…
findings.evidenceJa: 故に、日に二百以上の矢数をかけよ……とかなんとか。
findings.governingReading: Therefore, it says something like, “shoot at least two hundred arrows a day,” or words to that effect.
findings.explanation: The source's 二百以上 means at least 200, whereas “more than 200” excludes exactly 200. とかなんとか also explicitly marks the wording as approximate and half-remembered, but the English presents the instruction as a clean remembered quotation despite the source's repeated uncertainty markers. This makes Shirou's recollection both numerically stricter and more exact than it is.

findings.highlight: After letting magical energy flow throughout my body, I start the “strengthening” magic like always.
findings.evidenceJa: 全身に魔力を通したら、あとはお決まりの“強化”の練習。
findings.governingReading: After running magical energy through his whole body, all that remains is the usual practice of “strengthening.”
findings.explanation: The source labels what follows as practice or training of strengthening. The English turns this into starting the “strengthening” magic itself, which can imply he is already casting the spell rather than practicing a technique that he only recently regained.

findings.highlight: The magic that I succeeded at for the first time in a few years last night.
findings.evidenceJa: 昨夜、ランサーに襲われて何年かぶりに成功した強化の魔術。
findings.governingReading: It is the strengthening magecraft that succeeded last night, after Lancer attacked him, for the first time in several years.
findings.explanation: The English omits Lancer's attack, omits the explicit identification of the magecraft as strengthening, and leaves a malformed fragment (“the magic that I succeeded at”). The source ties the renewed success directly to the attack and to a specific spell discipline.
